title: Who owns what an AI was trained on?

turns.speaker: Gil
turns.text: The illustrators' case went to trial this week. Whether training on their work without asking was ever lawful.

turns.speaker: Ty
turns.text: The defence is that reading isn't copying. A person can look at ten thousand drawings and learn a style, and style isn't protected.

turns.speaker: Sana
turns.text: That analogy does a lot of work, though. A person reads slowly, forgets most of it, and can't be run ten million times in parallel.

turns.speaker: Gil
turns.text: Scale as a difference in kind rather than degree.

turns.speaker: Sana
turns.text: I think so, yes. The law usually cares about market effect, and this affects the market in a way one student never could.

turns.speaker: Ty
turns.text: The awkward part is that licensing everything would only be affordable for the biggest companies.

turns.speaker: Ty
turns.text: So a rule meant to protect artists ends up entrenching whoever can pay for a catalogue.

turns.speaker: Gil
turns.text: That's the strongest counter and I've never heard a good answer to it.

turns.speaker: Sana
turns.text: Collective licensing, maybe. It's how radio pays for music without negotiating with every band.

turns.speaker: Gil
turns.text: That took decades and a lot of legislation to build.

turns.speaker: Ty
turns.text: The part that gets lost is that most artists aren't asking for money first. They asked to be able to say no.

turns.speaker: Sana
turns.text: Which an opt-out does badly, because it assumes you knew it was happening.

turns.speaker: Gil
turns.text: And nobody did until the models were already trained.

points: Illustrators are litigating over whether training on their work without permission was lawful.
The defence argues learning a style is not copying, since style is unprotected.
Sana argues scale makes it a difference in kind, because the market effect exceeds anything a human learner could cause.
Ty's counter is that mandatory licensing would favour the largest companies, entrenching those who can buy catalogues.
Sana proposes collective licensing on the radio model, though Gil notes it took decades to establish.
Ty observes most artists sought the right to refuse rather than payment, which opt-out schemes handle poorly since nobody knew training was happening.
